This paper introduces a novel time-dependent Poisson autoregression model designed to capture both mean and volatility clustering in count data. We establish conditions ensuring non-explosiveness and prove the existence of a causal stationary solution. Furthermore, we develop consistent estimators for the time-dependent regression coefficients and asymptotic normality for the mean function. To address the unknown variance function, we propose a simple bootstrap method for constructing confidence intervals for the coefficient estimates and testing the significance of the time-dependent regression parameters. The theoretical findings are illustrated using daily data on the number of posts on the Chinese social media platform Weibo involving the entity Ukraine. Additionally, a R package with the same name has been created to facilitate the practical application of this model.

Atmospheric turbulence hinders astronomical observations by distorting light and degrading image quality. Over the past decade, we have implemented a technique to quantify this distortion for individual stars by analyzing the photometric variations of point-source stars through thin aerosol layers. This method, termed stellar photometric tomography (SPT), reconstructs the vertical structure of these aerosol layers. Applying SPT to the seeing issues faced by the TREC (Turbulence Robust Eye-Coronagraph) coronagraph, we developed a real-time correction system specifically for guide star photometry. When integrated into adaptive optics (AO) systems, this integration enhances overall image quality. Given that star photometry is extensively used across various scientific fields, it is reasonable to expect similar correction methods will be applied to improve the precision of star photometric variability measurements. Furthermore, we plan to utilize this correction to refine astrometric determinations from interferometric instruments like GRAVITY+ and future missions such as EXPOSE. Beyond these specific applications, we argue that SPT can be incorporated into other techniques designed to measure astronomical image blur, including Shack-Hartmann sensors and shape sensors employed in coronagraphs. Although SPT adds noise—drawing from photon statistics already allocated to target star images—this noise level is likely acceptable for many scenarios. As seen with our success in correcting guide star photometry for tip-tilt errors, we anticipate similar success when addressing higher-order wavefront distortions. While the required integration time depends on the specific application, current technology enables reconstruction rates of up to a few hertz. Looking ahead, more sophisticated tomographic methods could potentially replace SPT, particularly as space-based telescopes prepare to perform high-precision planetary coronagraphy, demanding extremely accurate characterization of on-line-of-sight atmospheric turbulence. This document details how we implemented Stellar Photometric Tomography and evaluates its potential for enhancing the precision of astronomical measurements.

We introduce a robust and efficient algorithm for sampling configurational space through a hybrid Monte Carlo approach that integrates molecular dynamics with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. This method proves particularly effective for samples drawn from conditional distributions, addressing the significant challenge of maintaining constant temperature in local conditions, such as local pressure, to enable sampling under combined temperature and pressure constraints. The algorithm's efficacy and rapid convergence are demonstrated through simulations of a Lennard-Jones fluid and a Lennard-Jones solid. Additionally, we apply this method to a Lennard-Jones mixture to investigate the phase behavior of a gas-liquid mixture under specific conditions. These simulations also reveal the algorithm's efficiency and fast convergence when dealing with Lennard-Jones mixture systems. The proposed technique offers a valuable tool for exploring configurational space in Lennard-Jones mixtures and other materials, potentially aiding in the discovery of novel materials and optimizing their processing conditions. This study conducts a qualitative analysis of these datasets to evaluate their actual quality and realism. The findings indicate that many entries lack naturalness and realism, suggesting that systems judged against these datasets may appear to perform well without actually producing natural image descriptions. This study examines the equation of state for hadronic matter under conditions of temperature and baryon chemical potential relevant to heavy-ion collisions, focusing on the phase transition from hadrons to quark-gluon plasma. The analysis employs a grand canonical statistical hadron gas model, constrained by the measured total baryon density and entropy per baryon. Beyond confirming previous findings that the transition temperature decreases with increasing entropy per baryon ($s$), the research identifies a second phase transition occurring at lower densities for entropies $s\lesssim 5$. At this transition, the dominant change involves the emergence of meson excitons, which do not contribute to the baryon number. Projected central baryon densities at beam energies of 7, 40, 100, and 200 GeV indicate that this excitation transition will occur during Au+Au collisions at 40 GeV and, potentially, during p+Pb collisions at 7 GeV. These events are expected to manifest as anomalous enhancements of light mesons, particularly $\eta$ and $\omega$. Such signals could be investigated in future experiments at the upgraded Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and at the Fixed-Field Alternating Gradient (FFAG) accelerator under development in Japan. Additionally, at 7 GeV, the baryon density during central Au+Au collisions will likely exceed the threshold required for quark-gluon matter formation; however, this state will be short-lived due to the low entropy per baryon at this energy and density. Consequently, the excitation transition and the onset of quark-gluon matter represent two distinct phenomena that could be explored in future fixed-target and high-energy heavy-ion collisions.

This paper introduces the feasibility of integrating data and energy delivery (IDED) systems utilizing single-carrier (SC) waveform characteristics for broad-bandwide operations, potentially reaching the GHz range. We examine the ideal SC-IDD system, outlining its fundamental principles and key performance indicators. Furthermore, we propose implementable variants of the SC-IDD, termed practical-IDD, and develop an optimal training scheme to establish performance benchmarks. We also develop a joint optimization algorithm to determine the ideal system design parameters. Through simulations, we compare the ideal and practical IDD schemes against a hybrid approach that combines time-division multiple access (TDMA) and orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM). Our results indicate that an IDD system with a 500 MHz bandwidth, serving a single user via a single antenna, can achieve both higher data rates and greater harvested energy than a TDMA-T-OFDM system utilizing a 1 GHz bandwidth with two radio heads (RH). Additionally, the data rate of an IDC system with a 500 MHz bandwidth can exceed that of an OC system operating over a 1 GHz bandwidth. These findings demonstrate that broadening bandwidth and employing carrier-based integration strategies like IDD and IDC are more effective than simply increasing the number of antennas or carriers for improving system performance. Finally, we consider the extension of these ideas to multi-user environments and anticipate future research directions in this area. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands a methodology that integrates statistical analysis with rigorous theoretical considerations. While the specific theoretical choices—such as the selected factorization scale, matching scheme, and evolution equation—do not influence the underlying statistical fit, they directly affect the resulting PDFs and their uncertainties. Consequently, a unified framework capable of fitting PDFs across different schemes and orders is both advantageous and necessary. This document presents such a framework, detailing the necessary theoretical and statistical components. We offer a comprehensive overview of the involved theories, outlining their interconnections and the mathematical transformations required to convert between them. Furthermore, we describe the practical implementation, covering the conversion of data from various experiments and theoretical sources, the formulation of data vectors, and the construction of the covariance matrix. Finally, we examine the calculation of errors and confidence levels, providing a consistent approach for assessing uncertainties. The implementation of this framework within the TROID software is also discussed. Although designed for PDF fits, this framework is broadly applicable to any analysis involving data transformation and error evaluation, serving as a valuable tool for combining diverse datasets. We conclude by highlighting several potential use cases. The source file for this document is troid_source.tex, which utilizes the nosection class option to prevent automatic heading creation and the glossaries package for defining and listing terminology; access to this file is available at https://github.com/TROID-framework/Theory-framework-for-PDF-fitting-.tex. Key terms and definitions include: all-order, confidence-level, factorization-scale, Fitter, matching-scheme, parton-distribution-function, PDF, statistical-analysis, theory-framework, trivial-relation, uncertainty, and UUncertainty. Additional glossary entries are available in the corresponding PDF version of this document.

This study employs a linearized model to examine how a turbulent methane-air jet flame reacts to inlets acoustic forcing within a rectangular duct. Using Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) on direct numerical simulation (DNS) data, the reaction to vertical acoustic modes is analyzed. The results indicate that higher-order modes exhibit weaker responses, a finding corroborated by the linearized heat release POD spectrum. Furthermore, the simulation data confirms that the flame's reaction aligns with the superposition of the specific acoustic mode being excited. These results support the validity of the linearized model for describing flame reactions to inlet acoustic forcing at amplitudes up to 5%. Within an active fire framework, this linearized model serves as a robust tool for investigating flame instabilities and oscillations. Furthermore, when integrated with a linearized turbulence model, it enables the exploration of instability mechanisms driven by turbulent fluctuations. Distinct from POD, this integration allows for a comprehensive analysis of heat release fluctuations across a broad spectrum of turbulent and acoustic frequencies. As a linear model, it also facilitates the calculation of coherent structures, such as eigenmodes, to identify potential flame oscillation modes. The study validates this approach by calculating the first axisymmetric acoustic mode and its associated heat release fluctuations, confirming that these fluctuations correspond to the higher-order POD mode $PO(2,1)$. Finally, the research demonstrates how to incorporate linearized acoustic and turbulence models into an $N$-mode decomposition framework to analyze heat release fluctuations via a modal decomposition approach.

Nonlocal gravity represents an effective field theory derived from underlying local theories, potentially as a consequence of UV completion via extra dimensions, analogous to how hydrodynamics emerges from kinetic theory. In this framework, the theory operates nonlocally through a convolution involving a kernel that functions as a propagator in extra dimensions, converting spacetime nonlocality into an extra-dimensional locality. This kernel, or propagator, is determined by a specific UV completion and defines a constitutive relation dependent on the deformation of spacetime. Similar to how the shear viscosity coefficient characterizes hydrodynamics, a coefficient describing the strength of nonlocality in gravity should ideally remain small; however, current observational constraints indicate that this coefficient is likely larger than anticipated. This paper reviews the formulation of nonlocal gravity, emphasizing the kernel and constitutive relation, and analyzes recent observational limits on the nonlocality coefficient. It also introduces a formalism for investigating anisotropic nonlocality and explores its potential implications for dark matter. Additionally, the work examines the connection between nonlocality and extra dimensions, proposing a method to estimate the scale of nonlocality based on the radius of curvature of extra dimensions. Finally, the authors introduce a formalism to assess the validity range of linear nonlocal gravity. Throughout, the discussion utilizes a teleparallel approach to describe nonlocal gravity. While proton-proton collisions at the LHC are dominated by minimal final states like Drell--Plan, $W$--Plan, and photon--Plan, these events constitute a significant minority. This paper examines the production of various other minor final states, ranking them by cross section. We outline methods to detect these rare events and highlight their potential utility for new physics searches. Specifically, we propose using these minor states to measure the mass of a new heavy resonance, a technique that could remain viable even if the resonance itself is too faint to be directly observed. We also suggest employing these final states to determine the luminosity of fixed-target experiments created by beam dumps or through colliding a proton beam with a laser, thereby linking the LHC to these facilities. We address the significance of rare, long-term non-outburst intervals in X-ray variable sources at the Galactic Centre, with a specific focus on identifying previously unrecognized low-mass X-ray binaries. Initially, we develop a statistical framework to examine transient activity among known star-forming galaxy accreting black holes, utilizing the Recurrence Interval Survey (RISurvey) dataset from the Chandra X-ray Survey of the Centaurus A galaxy. This approach yields a distribution of recurrence intervals for these systems and supports the hypothesis that these intervals stem from temporary accretion pauses caused by stellar companion stars. Adopting this model for the Galactic Centre's neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries, we analyze the distribution of intervals observed over the past two decades among known active sources. This examination reveals that the distribution of inactivity durations among previously detected systems aligns with the distribution of intervals for previously active sources now in quiescence, suggesting a uniform distribution across all systems. Consequently, we predict the imminent reactivation of two systems that have remained inactive for extended periods: GX 3.0+2, which has been quiet for over 15 years, and 4U 1608−52, inactive for more than a decade. Furthermore, we investigate the distribution of mass accretion rates between the previously active sources and those in quiescence, arguing that this distribution, combined with the lack of detectable optical emission in certain systems, indicates a minimum mass accretion rate below which X-ray binaries enter a "super-quiescent" state where optical lines disappear and X-ray emission falls under $10^{-3}$ of the Eddington limit. Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two distinct sets of entities. A graph $G$ admits a balanced chromatic vertex splitting (B-CVS) if a complete graph $K_n$ can be decomposed into homomorphisms of $G$ that partition the edges of $K_n$, where $n$ equals the product of the independent set sizes of $G$'s two parts. This paper demonstrates that a specific class of star-like bipartite graphs satisfies B-CVS, utilizing an FPT approach based on a known result by Gyori, Lehel, Tuza, and Yang. Additionally, we identify a further class of bipartite graphs for which deciding if B-CVS exists is W(1)-complete. Numerous additional star-like and bistar-like graphs are investigated regarding their B-CVS properties, and a collection of potential research directions is presented. The study also involves examining the HOM-MATRIX (homomorphism matrix) of a graph and defining its BISTAR-like graphs. Key questions addressed include: How can we decompose the edges of complete graphs into the homomorphisms of a specific bipartite graph's families? What characteristics must a bipartite graph possess to enable a complete graph edge decomposition into its homomorphisms? Which graph families allow for such decompositions, and what obstacles arise when they do not fit these categories? What constitutes an appropriate edge decomposition for a complete graph, and how can it be achieved? What is the precise definition of chromatic vertex splitting for a graph? Which graphs qualify as bistar-like, and how does this classification relate to the goal of decomposing complete graph edges into homomorphisms of a given bipartite graph? What constitutes a star-like graph, and what role does it play in this context? Finally, what are the practical applications of decomposing complete graph edges into the homomorphisms of a specific bipartite graph? It is also considered whether a graph $G$ can be decomposed to a complete graph's edges and what implications this has for determining if $G$ possesses B-CVS. This work also explores fixed-parameter tractable methods for bipartite graphs, the feasibility of B-CVS, and the necessary conditions and definitions involved in these concepts. Potential applications of these ideas are also discussed.

High-performance workloads demand fast CPU frequencies for optimal execution. However, existing CPUs operate below their maximum frequencies due to thermal and power constraints, creating a bottleneck that limits overall system performance. To address this, we introduce HyperDegrade, a technique that intentionally pushes CPU frequencies beyond their hardware limits to enhance performance for performance-critical workloads. By optimizing task scheduling and managing thermal constraints, HyperDegrade ensures that higher frequencies yield genuine performance gains. Our evaluations demonstrate that workloads running at frequencies 1.5 times lower than their peak can achieve performance improvements of up to 25% through HyperDegrade. Additionally, workloads already executing at or near their maximum frequency have been shown to gain an extra 17% performance. These results indicate that CPUs operating significantly below their optimal frequency can benefit from HyperDegrade, whereas those already close to their limit can see modest but meaningful enhancements. Furthermore, we provide guidelines for selecting the most effective frequency for HyperDegrade based on specific thermal headroom and workload characteristics. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first attempt at executing workloads at frequencies exceeding their nominal hardware capabilities. The open-source implementation of HyperDegrade is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/HyperDegrade.

This paper examines a game theory problem where two teams of agents must complete tasks spread across a regular graph, such as a grid or torus. The graph's structure defines the movement rules for each agent. While one team aims to occupy as many tasks as possible, the other team tries to stop them. Because the teams have different objectives, the game is zero-sum. We introduce a stochastic team formation strategy where agents do not know the exact state of the graph but rely on a first-order belief state. This approach is paired with a novel zero-sum game that uses a matrix derived from a Markov Decision Process (MDP). The results show that for any regular graph, the proposed strategy and game yield higher payoffs than the optimal mixed strategy used in previous work, which relied on the true Markovian state. These findings are particularly beneficial when the graph is complex, as the first team can secure more tasks than the second team can prevent. Simulations on both 1D and 2D regular graphs confirm the effectiveness of this strategy and game. The main advantages over prior methods are that the agent formation strategy performs better than the traditional optimal mixed strategy, and the new strategy/game combination delivers superior results than the former on complex regular graphs. These outcomes are significant because the formation strategy is easier to implement in practice, and the game provides a more realistic model of the uncertainty between teams. Ultimately, this research has applications in areas like search and rescue operations, planetary exploration, and military missions. The key contributions are the introduction of the multi-task synchronization game and the development of the corresponding first-time agent formation strategy and game. These innovations offer practical benefits: the formation strategy is more effective and easier to implement than earlier methods, and the game provides a more realistic representation of inter-team uncertainties. Additionally, the results demonstrate that the formation strategy outperforms the traditional team approach, while the game offers a more accurate depiction of uncertainty between the two teams. This paper presents an embedding technique for a group $G$ acting on a Cartesian product $X\times Y$ of two sets into a wreath product $H\times K$ of two groups, where $H$ acts on $X$ and $K$ acts on $Y$. This Cartesian breakdown method yields new results regarding the embedding of classical groups and their variants into different wreath products. These applications include resolving a question posed by Tomkinson about the embedding of symmetric and bijective non-degenerate groups into partial wreath products, as well as answering affirmatively a query from Willemsen about embedding full and bijective non-degenerate groups into partial wreath products. Additionally, this approach offers a solution to a problem from Willemsen concerning the embedding of orthogonal groups into various wreath products. It also enables the combination of previously unrelated embedding problems into groups via direct products, producing novel outcomes in this area. The applications of this embedding strategy are extensive and continue to develop; further developments will be covered in the accompanying paper \cite{LuczMuzamLaminx99}. Distinct from the direct sum decomposition of automorphisms of Cartesian products explored by Willemsen \cite{Willemsendirect}, this work focuses on decomposing groups rather than their automorphisms. Other approaches to embedding groups into wreath products, such as those by Luczak and Pyber \cite{LuczakyPyber93} or Willemsen \cite{WillemsenWreath}, are not utilized in this research. Finally, this paper does not address the problem of determining when a group is a specific wreath product variant, which was solved by Tomkinson \cite{Tomkinson1,Tomkinson2,Tomkinson3,Tomkinson4}.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise, a challenge that will become increasingly significant as current detectors approach their design sensitivities. To address this, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer (SSI), a novel topology that offers superior high-frequency sensitivity compared to both Michelson interferometers and previous non-reciprocal designs like the free-reciprocal interferometer. In this configuration, the high-frequency sensitivity surpasses the original Michelson's level by a factor of $|\beta|$, where $\beta$ represents the ratio of arm lengths. Assuming the longer arm in an upgraded Michelson detector is approximately 1000 meters, an existing 4 kilometer SSI could achieve a strain sensitivity of $10^{-20}$ at 10 MHz. This represents an improvement of nearly an order of magnitude over the sensitivity expected for a conventional Michelson detector with a 4 kilometer longer arm. The feasibility of implementing such a detector is evaluated, and potential applications for gravitational wave astronomy are discussed. Extra-large multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for addressing the challenges of massive wireless networks, particularly in terms of connectivity and spectrum efficiency. This study examines the visibility region (VR) of a set of access points (APs) serving the geometric distribution of user equipments (UEs) within a cell, and it evaluates the performance of a blind XL-MIMO protocol for handling user association during the initial phase. The findings indicate that the non-intersecting VR of UEs within a cell constitutes a significant portion of the overall VR. Consequently, this paper proposes a novel, simple, and effective protocol designed to manage the non-intersecting VR and enhances system throughput. Although neural models have largely supplanted $n$-gram models in language modeling due to superior performance, we demonstrate that simple neural networks can achieve the accuracy of substantial $n$-gram models by leveraging an explicit $n$-gram component. Specifically, we introduce a residual learning framework where a compact neural network learns to correct the errors of an underlying explicit $n$-gram model. This hybrid approach surpasses a wide range of standalone neural models, including prominent architectures like T5, BART, and GPT-2, across multiple downstream tasks. The framework is highly scalable; for instance, a model trained on Wikipedia using an 11-gram language model contains only 220 million parameters and outperforms Transformer-TF*, a 2022 state-of-the-art 3000-million parameter model. Additionally, the method requires no special hardware, as the explicit $n$-gram component is computed purely algorithmically. We further extend this approach to neural text generation, where the explicit $n$-gram component is derived from a back $n$-gram model. Our experiments indicate that this residual framework effectively mitigates the degradation in generation quality typically caused by using a back $n$-gram component. This study evaluates Informed OCR (iOCR), a method designed to correct errors in conventional OCR systems when processing ballot images for vote tabulation. We assessed the systems using the IBOV metric, which quantifies the impact of character identification errors on the final ballot count. The evaluation took place in a real-world setting involving over 130,000 scanned ballots from a recent municipal election in an Indian city. Results demonstrate that IOCR significantly outperforms standard OCR approaches, achieving an improvement of more than a factor of two in IBOV. Additionally, the evaluations provided insights into the limitations of both traditional and informed OCR. Given that no error-free "out-of-the-box" OCR solution exists for ballots, the open-source iOCR project offers a practical alternative to standard OCR for ballot image analysis during tallying operations. The system is accessible at https://github.com/imes-bitsuites/IOCRAge. ( authored by A. K. Singh). (See also arXiv:2001.09603 and 2001.05606).

This study investigates the atmospheric circulation patterns of terrestrial planets using a simple general circulation model. The model incorporates anisotropic eddy viscosity and drag, along with radiative cooling rates that vary by altitude and latitude. We examine how equatorial super-rotation emerges and transitions into turbulence as stellar insolation, eddy viscosity, and angular momentum vary. Additionally, we explore the influence of anisotropic eddy viscosity and drag on circulation structures, identifying a critical role for poleward eddy viscosity in generating baroclinic eddies and driving mid-latitude jets. Findings from this work, combined with those of the accompanying paper, align well with observed wind patterns on gas giants and offer potential applications to exoplanetary atmospheres. The research utilizes the spectral global climate model GENESIS, which features anisotropic eddy viscosity and drag parameterized as functions of potential vorticity and Rossby deformation radius, alongside a cooling rate dependent on latitude and temperature. Distinct circulation regimes are identified based on the Froude number (Fr), representing the ratio of centrifugal to Coriolis acceleration caused by stellar insolation, and the non-dimensional eddy turnover time ($\tau_{\eta}$). These regimes, ordered from low to high Fr and low to high $\tau_{\eta}$, are termed: balanced super-rotation, cyclostrophic super-rotation, baroclinic eddy dominance, geostrophic eddy dominance, and turbulent dominance. This classification mirrors the traditional hydrodynamic ordering by Reynolds number and corresponds to the astrophysical ordering by Prandtl and Rossby numbers. For Theia, a terrestrial planet with 1.5$\times$ Earth's gravity, 1.25$\times$ Earth's radius, and 2$\times$ Earth's insolation, the analysis predicts a primary mid-latitude jet accompanied by a weak equatorial super-rotating gyre, a structure similar to what is observed on Earth and Jupiter. Similarly, for a Mars-like planet with identical insolation but lower angular momentum, the predicted pattern consists of two strong mid-latitude jets with only a minimal equatorial super-rotating gyre, which aligns with wind data from Mars. These results indicate that baroclinic eddies play a dominant role in determining the circulation patterns of Theia, Mars, and other terrestrial planets with low insolation or high gravity, while cyclostrophic balance primarily governs highly irradiated rocky exoplanets and the atmospheres of gas giants. We introduce a stochastic hydrodynamic theory derived from the Wigner function through a randomization of phase space, analogous to the Nelsonian approach for quantum hydrodynamics in classical many-body systems. This method, termed the M-S-H formalism, incorporates quantum effects via a spacetime non-Gaussianity measure representing quantum diffusion. Similar to the Lewis-Riesenfeld formalism, quantum effects manifest as a deterministic evolution of this measure driven by an integro-differential integral collision term within the governing stochastic hydrodynamic equations. We demonstrate that for free gases, this term vanishes, allowing for a first-principles derivation of a spacetime non-Gaussianity measure with specific initial conditions. Extending this to interacting gases requires assuming the measure's form based on free gas results and estimating the collision term under that assumption. As with the Lewis-Riesenfeld formalism, this constitutes an approximation; however, we provide justification for its validity. Applying this framework to Bose gases, we derive a set of hydrodynamic equations that include quantum effects and thermal fluctuations, the latter arising from the integration over initial microscopic stochastic variables. These equations resemble those from mean-field theories, such as two-fluid models or mean-field kinetic theories like BUU or QBUU, but additionally account for quantum phenomena like tunneling. Consequently, they may serve as a practical alternative to microscopic methods like the Wigner-Kholsmakovsky Liouville equation in certain contexts. Finally, we outline how to incorporate superfluidity into this model.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various fields, yet their high dimensionality and parameter counts often create significant deployment challenges when applied to real-world scenarios. To address this, Knowledge Learning (KL) has emerged as a promising alternative that enables systems to acquire human knowledge from large-scale data without requiring massive parameter volumes. By integrating external knowledge sources—such as databases and pre-trained models—into their architectures, KL systems can effectively tackle complex tasks like image recognition and natural language understanding. These systems typically operate using a two-phase workflow: a knowledge construction phase, where a source model learns from data to generate a representation, followed by a construction-inference phase, where a target model utilizes this representation for inference. To enable this, specialized components known as Instructors and Students are employed; the Instructor processes raw data while the Student learns from the Instructor's outputs. Despite the widespread adoption of this framework, designing effective Instructors and Students remains difficult, as the Instructor's role extends beyond simply generating representations. Crucially, the Instructor must align the data distribution with the Student's input distribution, ensure the data is suitable for the target application, and guarantee that the Student can actually learn from it. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the Instructor-Student (I-S) architecture, detailing its application across various knowledge sources and both Image and Text domains. Furthermore, it introduces a novel I-S architecture called Knowledge Network (KN), which incorporates a knowledge module between the Instructor and Student. This module is trained independently and offers flexible, customizable knowledge integration. Our findings indicate that the KN architecture outperforms traditional I-S approaches in terms of learning efficiency and generalization capabilities. To facilitate future research, we have developed an open-source Python library called "Instructor-Student Framework" (ISF), which implements multiple I-S methods alongside our proposed KN architecture. The ISF framework supports various knowledge sources and Instructor types, making it a valuable resource for academic investigation and practical deployment. Ultimately, this survey and our proposed architecture have the potential to advance both the study of Knowledge Learning and its real-world applications. The accompanying video provides a visual overview of this survey: https://youtu.be/17s01111111. Our dataset and source code are accessible at: https://github.com/DeepBrainVT/Instructor-Student_Framework_for_Knowledge_Learning.

We introduce a novel exact inference algorithm for Markov decision processes (MDPs) and constrained optimization problems, leveraging a new function representation that accelerates value iteration by an order of magnitude. We establish theoretical bounds demonstrating that this representation uses linearly less memory than standard approaches. Additionally, we present a comparable representation for utility functions in mean-payoff games, which enables the application of other algorithms to analyze games on large graphs. Leveraging this, we define a bottom-up algorithm to determine winning regions for agents or processes subject to fairness or mean-payoff constraints; when combined with a state-space reduction technique, this creates a top-down algorithm capable of solving such games entirely. Our experimental results confirm the efficiency of this end-to-end approach for both fair mean-payoff games and general mean-payoff games. Furthermore, our revised value iteration algorithms for MDPs and Markov games are significantly faster than previous state-of-the-end methods, a benefit we utilize to derive improved bounds for mean fair-mean-payoff games and general mean-payoff games. These refined bounds reveal, for instance, that deciding whether a mean-payoff fairness constraint is satisfiable under a specific priority constraint is PSPACE-complete when the agent has access to imperfect information. All of our proposed algorithms are open-sourced at https://github.com/Asad Khan1337/FRPE.

Significant multiple testing issues arise when analyzing baseball teams' batting and pitching orders using paired-permutation tests. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a step-down paired-permutation method that maintains strong control over family-wise error rates. We demonstrate that this approach possesses sufficient power to identify statistically significant differences between structured alternatives, such as various batting and pitching sequences. To facilitate this, we develop a uniform testing framework for families of hypotheses involving both restricted and unrestricted permutations. This framework enables the construction of heterogeneous test statistics with differing powers, which are then balanced through step-down procedures to ensure optimal significance rates for each specific hypothesis. The efficacy and robustness of this new method are illustrated through applications to baseball problems and additional examples. Ultimately, we outline several open questions regarding further applications of the step-down paired-permutation framework in statistics, data science, and beyond. This work serves as a companion to /davidson2022deepbat/. The code is accessible at https://github.com/maristatistics/PrecisePairedPermutation. Keywords: family-wise error rate; multiple testing; step-down procedure; structured data; baseball; permutation testing; paired-data.

The measured suppression of the third-order elliptic flow, $v_3$, in Au+Au collisions by approximately a factor of two relative to $v_2$ suggests that initial geometric anisotropy in non-central heavy-ion collisions significantly drives $v_3}$, while the hydrodynamic response remains proportional to the initial anisotropy. To examine this hypothesis using a multiphase transport (AMPT) model, we first analyzed the $p_T$ dependence of $v_n$ in central Au+Au collisions to calibrate the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$) of the fluid. Subsequently, we investigated $v_3}$ in non-central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions by adjusting the initial $\eta/s$ specifically for those events. Our results indicate that the $v_3}/v_2$ ratio in non-central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions within the AMPT framework is highly sensitive to the initial $\eta/s$. Furthermore, when the initial $\eta/s$ for non-central events is set higher than that of central Au+Au collisions, the ratio $v_3}/v_2$ aligns well with experimental data. These findings support the conclusion that a relatively larger initial $\eta/s}$ in non-central compared to central heavy-ion collisions contributes to the lower $v_3}$ observed in the latter. Additionally, the results demonstrate that the anisotropic pressure gradients in non-central collisions are insufficient to fully account for the $v_3}$ magnitude, implying that initial state anisotropies play a crucial role. Finally, we observed that increasing the initial $\eta/s}$ enhances the $v_3}/v_2$ ratio while reducing $v_3}$ itself, a trend consistent with experimental observations.

This study introduces a Poisson multi-Birahimovich-Measars-Malevics (PMBRM) filter tailored for birth-and-death processes on nearly grid-based spaces, featuring a novel state-space partition. This approach enables efficient implementation of PMBM dynamics, particularly in birth and death processes, by aligning with a discrete-time Markov chain Monte Carlo filter (like PHD-MCMC) for specific regions. The proposed method is demonstrated in a sensor management framework comprising a peltian multiagent team operating within a largely grid-like environment. First, optimal actions are calculated using a myopic multiagent Monte Carlo simulation, followed by the PMBM filter for multiagent birth-and-death processes outside the main search area. This final step ensures computational feasibility. Simulations reveal that the new PMBRM filter effectively tracks multiagent birth-and-death processes in largely discrete environments, surpassing traditional PMBM filter efficiency in such scenarios. Additionally, the study derives PMBM dynamics for birth-and-death processes in specific regions, offering a practical technique for handling these processes in targeted areas. These derived dynamics are validated through other simulations, confirming their accuracy. Ultimately, this work provides a significant contribution to literature on multiagent estimation, control, and coordination, with potential applications in air traffic control, search and rescue operations, and similar domains. The detailed state-space description for this PMBM filter with a mostly discrete environment is illustrated in Figure 1. Notably, this paper does not utilize point processes; all derivations are based on regular measures. Consequently, the novel PMBM dynamics with a mostly discrete state space and the associated regularized PMBM (R-PMBM) dynamics in this mostly grid-based setting represent new findings, distinct from conventional PMBM dynamics in those contexts. Furthermore, unlike standard PMBM processes, these novel dynamics allow for explicit computation of first-order densities on the mostly discrete state space, facilitating the derivation of regularized PMBM (R-PMBM) dynamics in this mostly grid-based environment. These r-pmbm dynamics can then be applied in a multiagent pmbrm framework for optimization and decision-making, similar to how r-bhma dynamics are used in a fully discrete multiagent r-bhma setting for coordination. Ultimately, this research delivers a significant advancement: a PMBM filter for mostly discrete state spaces, achieved by combining the state-space partition on the mostly grid-based area with a conventional Birmahers-Measars-Malevics (BRM) multiagent Monte Carlo method for the fully discrete region

Soccer teams are driven by the objective of scoring more goals than their opponents. Consequently, the decision-making processes of individual players significantly influence a team's overall success. We apply deep reinforcement learning (DL) to enhance the policies of specific soccer agents during critical match moments. Our approach utilizes a modified state-of-the-art model, MAPPO, integrating graph convolutional networks to process game statistics. When evaluated on a real-world soccer dataset, our method outperforms existing DL techniques in policy optimization. Furthermore, our model achieves higher rewards than MAPPO across different simulation environments, demonstrating superior performance in key scenarios compared to prior state-of-the-art solutions. Finally, the optimized policies exhibit improved decision-making during critical moments, a benefit particularly valuable for professional soccer teams. Open source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abdulrahman-alkhateeb/Towards-enhanced-actions-in-critical-situations-of-soccer-games-with-deep-reinforcement-learning.

This study presents a method to expand the measurement range of a single-source single-detector Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDLV) system, which is inherently limited to one-dimensional (1D) data collection. By integrating a simple 1D Camera (1DC) alongside the LDLLV setup, the system achieves a broader 2D measurement area through a technique termed "distant operation." In this approach, the LDLLV provides high-precision 1D vibration velocity data, while the 1DC captures the 2D spatial distribution of a light dot generated by a laser beam reflected from the target surface. The 1DC primarily determines the light dot's position to estimate the surface's 1D vibration velocity at a location beyond the direct reach of the LDLLV beam, effectively extending the overall 2D measurement range. Experimental results demonstrate that this configuration successfully acquired 2D velocity data over an area of 1.44 m² at a distance of 1.2 meters from the source. These findings confirm the method's feasibility and highlight its potential for cost-effective, wide-field 2D vibration monitoring. Furthermore, this low-cost solution offers a viable alternative for acquiring 2D velocity data at locations where conventional accelerometers or other LDLV configurations are impractical to deploy. We implemented a Monte Carlo simulation to solve the quantum harmonic oscillator driven by a classical force, employing both Metropolis-Hastings and heat-bath algorithms. We introduce a calculus of structural conjunctive HOARE reasoning extended with expectations, designed to verify safety and liveness properties of imperative programs. While expectations allow for safety verification, we demonstrate that structurally additive reasoning—utilizing boolean expectations and both conjunctive and additive operators—is essential for validating liveness. From this calculus, we derive a calculus of relational reasoning, enabling the derivation of hoop rules and expectations for safety and liveness verification without a priori defining specific satisfaction operators or their structures. Furthermore, we establish a rule for reasoning about program similarity, from which we derive rules for safety and liveness expectations. Finally, we define a metric on relational expressions and expectations to quantify the liveness properties of the associated hoare expressions and expectations. The calculus of structural conjunctive hoare reasoning with expectations is further generalized to incorporate probabilistic expectations and a probabilistic similarity metric, facilitating the verification of safety and probabilistic liveness for probabilistic programs. All reasoning rules are visualized as a monad of "conjunction," "safety expectation," and "additive expectation," followed by a probabilistic variant of this monad; these generalizations yield rules for verifying safety and probabilistic liveness in imperative and probabilistic programs. As an application, we derive an iteration rule for liveness verification of loops, leveraging the expectation and similarity lifting rules along with invariant, hoop, and similarity rules. The derivation of the liveness invariant rule requires a proof of the "congruence of similar terms" lemma, which relies on the metric defined over relational expressions and expectations. This paper introduces a framework for predicting views for unseen videos within the New View Video (NV) dataset, which comprises 1,813 previously unseen videos from 100 specific categories. The proposed approach begins by estimating the camera's orientation relative to a reference view through a two-step method: first, it forecasts views in a discrete grid, and second, derives the exact camera orientation using a regression network. We introduce the $k$-trimmed distance, which defines the maximum distance a vertex $v$ can be from a subset $S$ when measured along simple paths of length at most $k$. Consequently, the $k$-trimmed metric on a graph $G$ may no longer satisfy the metric axioms; specifically, the axiom $d(u,S)\leq d(u,v)+d(v,S)$ can fail. Therefore, we define the $k$-trimmed metric dimension as the minimum graph dimension compatible with the $k$-trimmed metric. Unlike the standard metric dimension, the 1-trimmed metric dimension is not always finite even for finite graphs. For $k\geq 2$, we establish that the 2-trimmed metric dimension of a tree is always finite. Furthermore, we determine the 2-trimmed metric dimension for path graphs and specific types of trees, and provide upper bounds for general graphs and trees. Finally, we characterize when the 2-trimmed metric dimension equals the ordinary metric dimension for trees. The concepts of $k$-trimmed metric, $k$-trimmed metric dimension, and related orders for graphs are illustrated with numerous examples. We frequently detect transitions of heavier molecules in the spectra of lower-luminosity galaxies that remain undetected in higher-luminosity galaxies, despite the latter being more likely to possess the dense molecular gas reservoirs required for such lines. A prime example is the $n = 3 \rightarrow 2$ and $n = 2 \rightarrow 1$ drops of atomic carbon (C{\ii}), observed in several galaxies. These transitions are intrinsically bright, representing the second and third brightest lines in the spectrum of cooled ($T_{\rm kin} \sim 20$\,K) molecular gas, making their absence in certain galaxies striking. In this work, we examine the physical conditions necessary to excite these lines, analyzing a sample of 28 galaxies with detected C{\ii}(2--1) using non-LTE modeling. We find that exciting these lines requires high gas densities ($n({\rm H}_2) \sim 10^3$\,cm$^{-2}$) and low kinematic temperatures ($T_{\rm kin} \lesssim 25$\,K). Consequently, the presence of C{\ii}(2--1) serves as a signature of efficient gas cooling within dense reservoirs, likely driven by strong star formation and/or recent gas inflows. While the C{\ii}(2--1) line can be a useful tracer of high-density, cool gas, its flux is not a reliable indicator of total gas mass or specific star formation rate. Furthermore, the C{\ii}(1--0) / (2--1) ratio is an unreliable metric for deriving kinematic gas temperatures due to the non-thermal nature of this relationship. Ultimately, the C{\ii}(2--1) line acts as a signature of extreme gas cooling rather than a direct probe of gas mass; therefore, its utility lies in facilitating comparisons of "specific gas cooling rate" between galaxies, offering insights into the drivers of their star formation activity. It remains uncertain if a dual mode of star formation exists, peaking between elliptical and lenticular galaxies. To investigate this, we examined the central outer specific SFR (sOsfrc) gradient in a sample of 10,144 early-type galaxies using MaNGA data. We confirmed the well-established turning over of the mass-to-age tracer (Gamma1) at high masses and found a similar turnover in the central specific SFR (osfrc). Conversely, the gradient of the central Dn(4000) index did not show a significant turnover at high masses, indicating that the sOsfrc is a more reliable indicator of recent star formation than Gamma1 or Dn(4000). We also analyzed the correlation between osfrc and metallicity, determining that the traditional "two sequences" pattern on the M*-sSFR diagram results from the combination of a constant central sOsfrc with rising metallicity at fixed mass and a turnover of the sOsfrc itself at high mass. Finally, we assessed the plausibility of this dual star formation model by comparing predicted and observed global properties, noting that while nuce* (a model incorporating central sOsfrc turnover as a function of density and metallicity) aligns better with data than mass-to-age models, significant discrepancies persist at both the lowest and highest masses. These gaps suggest that additional physical mechanisms beyond what nuce* accounts for are required to fully explain the global stellar properties of early-type galaxies. Nuce* models and predictions will be integrated into the simulation pipeline for the Euclid mission to define the usable range of the M*-Euclid_sFR relation. The outer layers of Jupiter rotate more slowly than its interior, a phenomenon likely caused by the migration and absorption of giant planets during the gas giant's formation. In this study, we investigate the spin profile of Taurus AB, a close binary system consisting of a collapsing low-mass star and a low-mass brown dwarf accreting mass from a circumstellar disk. High-resolution spectroscopic observations reveal that the brown dwarf's rotation profile is non-monotonic: its poles rotate slower than its mid-latitudes, which in turn rotate more slowly than its equator. This profile aligns with either the angular momentum deposition from a planet or star onto a body and suggests an internal structure similar to Jupiter's. Given the negligible spin of brown dwarfs, this represents the first observed non-monotonic rotation profile in a brown dwarf or planet. These findings support a formation model where a low-mass brown dwarf underwent a giant impact following the collapse of its circumstellar disk, or where a planet was engulfed by a brown dwarf. Alternatively, if neither impact nor planet engulfment occurred, the profile implies an unexpectedly complex mechanism for transporting angular momentum in the brown dwarf's interior. Further research is required to distinguish between these scenarios, as the resulting rotation profile could serve as a "smoking gun" for specific formation mechanisms. While deep learning models show promise in detecting news authenticity, their application to new domains is constrained by the vast volume of data required for training and labeling. Furthermore, generating labels for individual articles to classify them as genuine or fake is often challenging. This study introduces MetaFEND, a meta-learning framework designed to identify both existing manipulated articles and those that are merely misleading. To address data scarcity, the framework utilizes synthetic manipulated samples created through image editing and text modification techniques. As a meta-learning approach, it employs neural process networks for training; specifically, it incorporates a attention-based encoder and a meta-learned network to classify manipulated and fake news. The model operates on a one-shot learning paradigm, enabling it to detect misleading and fake content without domain-specific supervision. Evaluations conducted across two real-world datasets, TwitterTruth and RealToFake, demonstrate that MetaFEND outperforms state-of-the-art methods in few-shot learning scenarios. Additionally, the framework effectively handles unseen samples in multimodal news verification tasks by generating labels for both manipulated and fake categories through a combination of image and text processing. The meta-learned classifier also successfully identifies the category of new samples—determining whether they are authentic, misleading, or manipulated—and provides visualizations of the decision-making process for individual samples. These capabilities make the system particularly valuable for fact-checking organizations and social media platforms. Synthetic data serves as a crucial resource for developing algorithms tasked with detecting rare events, such as brain injuries in CT scans. However, existing methods often fall short in generating realistic samples from complex scenarios. This paper introduces a novel framework for synthesizing brain injury cases from CT images by integrating a variational auto-encoder (VAE) with two adversarial networks (GANs) in a progressive strategy. Initially, a general-purpose GAN is trained on healthy CT scans to create realistic outputs. Subsequently, a specialized VAE-GAN is applied to generate brain injury scenes, conditioned on the synthetic healthy images produced in the first stage. Finally, a second special GAN is utilized to ensure the realism of the CT images after the inversion process. As anticipated, this multi-step approach outperforms conventional single-GAN and single-VAE-GAN methods, with the VAI-GAN demonstrating superior performance across multiple metrics. The effectiveness of this framework is validated using two public brain injury datasets, and its practical utility is illustrated by enabling a minority-class sampling network to detect brain injuries in synthetic minority datasets. This paper introduces SKILL (Structured Knowledge Injection for Language Models), a technique that lifts these constraints to inject knowledge into pre-trained LLMs without requiring access to the original data sources. We present an end-to-end framework capable of injecting diverse knowledge sources, including knowledge graphs, taxonomies, and FAQ pairs, into both open-source foundation models and commercial APIs. For instance, we observed a 3.1-point increase in zero-shot factual question answering using MetaDataQA and a 2.4-point gain in few-shot TREC v2. Additionally, the framework effectively incorporates specialized knowledge from knowledge graphs and FAQs, leading to measurable improvements in related metrics. The source code and a pre-built toolkit supporting various knowledge types are available at https://github.com/IBM/skill-framework. This open-source tool enables the enrichment of LLMs with diverse structured knowledge, potentially yielding significant performance enhancements.

This study examines the acoustic emission (AE) spectrum of an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant speed and a gradually increasing lateral tension. Under specific tension ranges, the AE displays a distinct side-band structure. This phenomenon arises from the superposition of two primary frequencies: a impact frequency generated as the tape adheres at irregular intervals, and a saw-tooth wave frequency resulting from non-uniform peeling angles across different segments. By analyzing this side-band spectrum, it is possible to determine the impact frequency and consequently estimate the number of times the tape sticks and slips per second. Furthermore, a simple model is proposed to correlate the impact frequency with the lateral tension, offering insights into the dynamics of the stick-slip process. These findings provide valuable data for understanding noise patterns in materials that fracture under stress, such as brittle substances or damaged components. Additionally, the methodology of deriving impact frequency from a side-band spectrum, initially used here to quantify stick-slip dynamics in an adhesive tape, may be applicable to other systems exhibiting similar acoustic emission patterns during deformation or failure. Future research will focus on experimentally validating the model that links impact frequency with lateral tension. This work was conducted within the "Acoustic Emission: From Micro-Emission to Seismic Emission" special research project (No. 18JD022300) of the National Social Science Fund of China.

Neural networks, particularly convolutional ones, have achieved significant success in processing images and video due to the invariant properties of its filter-based architecture toward affine transformations. This same approach could be applied to point clouds; however, such methods struggle with the non-structured nature of point data and tend to overfit, rendering them unsuitable for real-world applications. In contrast, smoothing techniques from statistics and signal processing offer a promising alternative for handling point clouds, yet they have historically been underutilized because of difficulties in defining appropriate kernels. This paper introduces a novel linear preprocessing method called TPC: Transformation-Unique Smoothing specifically designed for point clouds. We integrate TPC into neural network architectures, proposing both a convolutional model and a graph-based model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that these models outperform state-of-the-art approaches on various point cloud classification and segmentation tasks. This paper presents a proof of the $l$-adic local Langlands correspondence for characters of the absolute Galois group attached to an inertial prime $p$, extending the result by Breuil and Méndez (2019) to a broader context. Additionally, we establish a reciprocity law linking the existence of Hecke eigenvalues for classical eigenforms at inertial primes to the congruences of their Coxeter numbers modulo $l$ at ramified primes. The demonstrations rely on explicit computations utilizing Kummer theory and the theory of Berghuijs, Breuil, and Conrad regarding potentially crystalline representations with non-semisimple restricted monodromy operators. These explicit constructions serve as the foundation for an alternative proof of the "weight zero" component of the Muirhead--Wiles strategy, which connects Eichler-Shimura congruences at inertial primes to Serre's definition of Hecke eigenvalues at ramified primes. This approach complements the method originally proposed by Serre.

This study presents a technique to precisely manage damage in self-sensing composite structures through electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and a genetic algorithm (GA). While micro-delaminations in fiber-reinforced polymer composites alter local electrical conductivity, accurately locating and characterizing these defects via conductivity inversion remains challenging due to the ill-posed nature of the problem. To overcome this, a two-step approach is proposed: a global genetic algorithm initially identifies the most probable damage zones based on a predefined search area, followed by a local optimization method that precisely determines the size and position of each delamination within those identified regions. The efficacy of this method is validated using an impact scenario involving multiple micro-delaminations in a cross-ply carbon fiber/Epoxy laminate. Results demonstrate that the combination of EIT and the optimized GA successfully identified delaminations with an average localization error under 10 mm and size errors below 5%. Furthermore, the study provides insights into the influence of initial GA parameters on the accuracy of damage characterization. These findings highlight the potential of this framework for precisely identifying multiple micro-delaminations, offering a valuable tool for quality control in additive manufacturing and for damage detection and repair in aerospace composite structures. We introduce two novel algorithms for involutory matrices and a generalization applicable to arbitrary matrices, designed to accelerate computationally intensive tasks on GPUs. These methods offer a significant computational advantage over conventional iterative approaches for invertible matrices, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios. Unlike traditional techniques that converge asymptotically to a solution, our approach does not require convergence. We demonstrate these algorithms across various matrix types, including general, symmetric, positive definite, involutory, and orthogonal matrices. Furthermore, we provide a practical application by enhancing the calculation of MMSE filters in wireless communication systems. Empirical results from 2019 reveal a speedup of over 100x compared to state-of-the-art methods for general matrices and approximately 3x for low-rank updates. For complex high-dimensional matrix inversions, our method is approximately 50 times faster than the best available alternative. We categorize these techniques into three groups: precomputed methods suitable for static matrices with accessible storage; rapidly computable approaches for dynamic matrices; and hybrid solutions that leverage the strengths of both.

We assume that both the feature vectors and reward values are bounded. Under these conditions, we introduce an iterative method that achieves a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{d\log(C_x\log(n))n})$, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the feature vectors, $C_x$ denotes the bound on their Euclidean norm, and $n$ is the total number of time steps. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism arising in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks due to gas heating by accretion and dust radiative cooling. As cooling becomes more efficient, the VSI growth rate increases, potentially leading to supersonic velocities that trigger gravitational collapse or shock formation; however, these processes may simultaneously suppress further instability growth. Given that dust settles and evolves over time, this progression could cause the VSI to transition from active to quiescent within a specific layer, potentially releasing accumulated supersonic turbulent motions into a broader region. To investigate these dynamics, we developed a 1.5D hydrodynamic model incorporating dust evolution, which we integrated with a simple turbulence model to estimate turbulent viscous stresses. Our results demonstrate that dust evolution significantly enhances turbulent stress in the outer disk regions. For a disk with an initial mass of 0.01 solar masses, the effective viscosity coefficient $\alpha$ ranges from $10^{-5}$ to $5\times10^{-4}$ depending on the initial gas temperature. These findings align with the $\alpha$ values required to account for the luminosity excess observed in the outer regions of young, massive disks. Furthermore, our derived relation between $\alpha$ and the initial gas temperature matches the trend inferred from the spectral energy distributions of a sample of classical T Tauri stars. We conclude that dust evolution plays a critical role in the VSI, thereby offering a solution to the long-standing challenge of explaining low outer disk masses alongside high accretion rates in the early stages of planet formation. The rise of machine learning systems in critical sectors has increased exposure to backdoor attacks, which introduce subtle manipulation during training to cause specific unintended behaviors under targeted triggers. Recently, adversaries have developed more efficient "dynamic" backdoors that operate without access to the training dataset. While prior research primarily relied on pixel-based triggers, this study explores dynamic backdoors utilizing global features as activation patterns. We demonstrate that neural networks employing global average pooling (e.g., ResNet) are susceptible to this new attack variant. In contrast, we show that a network using global mean *convolution* with a filter smaller than the input image dimensions can effectively resist dynamic backdoors. Furthermore, we provide evidence that a global mean convolution layer with a filter size matching the input dimensions offers no protection against this threat. Finally, we confirm that a global mean convolution with an oversized filter can successfully mitigate the attack, provided the final fully connected layer remains unchanged. Our findings highlight the necessity of carefully designing global feature extraction layers to ensure robustness against dynamic feature-based backdoor attacks. This paper addresses the challenge of training a global deep neural network (DNN) to perform classification on highly imbalanced, heterogeneous data using a Federated Learning (FL) framework. In this approach, only stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates are transmitted to the server, requiring an efficient method for processing such data distributions without exposing raw data or local models. We introduce a random walk (RW) based learning strategy where a RW agent learns local data distributions and identifies the optimal local classifier. Consequently, a central learning algorithm (ALA) guides the RW agent's path to access the most suitable local model for each data sample. We propose two specific RW patterns: directional RW (DRW) and spiral RW (SRW). Extensive simulations demonstrate that both DRW and SRW-FL significantly outperform existing methods in classification accuracy while reducing communication costs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Aniruddha-1997/RW-FL. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: (a) We formulated an optimization problem aiming to maximize classification accuracy under constraints on communication rounds and data volume, (b) We designed a central learning algorithm (ALA) and two random walk patterns (DRW and SRW) to solve this problem, (c) We theoretically proved that the proposed solution is near-optimal regarding classification accuracy, and (d) We validated our approach through simulations, showing that the random walk patterns effectively leverage data volume and communication round constraints to enhance classification performance on heterogeneous, imbalanced datasets. Although the concept of nonlocality was initially introduced to demonstrate that quantum mechanics contradicts local hidden variable theories, it is now recognized as a resource essential for specific tasks, such as enhancing communication complexity or enabling remote state preparation within protocols like teleportation. Similarly, single-particle entanglement, which arises from the correlation between parts of a superposed wavefunction, serves as a valuable tool for analogous objectives, including extending quantum communication complexity and facilitating certain remote quantum operations. This paper establishes that single-particle entanglement possesses sufficient strength to generate nonlocal effects and even allows for single-particle steering. We illustrate this by defining a single-particle quantum correlation based on measurement statistics and creating a "single-particle Bell inequality," which functions as the natural counterpart to the standard Bell inequality. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of single-particle steering and demonstrate its occurrence. Our analysis reveals that, just as with standard entanglement, both nonlocality and single-particle steering increase with degree, and we provide an explicit example of a single-particle Bell inequality violation that occurs only when entanglement exceeds a particular threshold. Finally, we present a practical application of the single-particle Bell inequality within a "witness" framework for verifying single-particle entanglement, and we show how both the single-particle Bell inequality and the phenomenon of single-particle steering can be utilized to elevate security in quantum key distribution protocols.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks widely employed for sequence processing tasks, such as speech recognition and video identification. By leveraging the hierarchical Tucker (HT) decomposition, a low-rank matrix decomposition technique, we compress the HT-structured LSTM weights to mitigate computational complexity.
